power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: Research on the impact of social media use on adolescent mental health lacks consensus, likely exacerbated by the field's reliance on coarse measures like time spent online.
More granular conceptualisations of use have been proposed as a way to clarify when, why, and for whom social media use may be beneficial, neutral, or harmful.
In this scoping review, we used the Multidimensional Model of Social Media Use (Yang et al., 2021) as a framework to systematically map the diversity of adolescent social media use.
text.formatted: In this scoping review, we used the Multidimensional Model of Social Media Use <ref type="bibr" target="#b85">(Yang et al., 2021)</ref> as a framework to systematically map the diversity of adolescent social media use.

text.text: Specifically, we examined how adolescents describe their social media use, how researchers quantify this use and the degree of (dis)alignment between the two.
In total, we reviewed 6,822 articles for inclusion, with 522 meeting the inclusion criteria.
Adolescents' qualitative accounts portrayed social media use as complex, fluid, and multi-dimensional, involving a wide range of activities, motivational functions, and communication partners.

We draw on these accounts to extend the Multidimensional Model, specifying more precise categories of activity, motivation, and communication partner, and incorporating additional contextual dimensions that characterise adolescents' social media use.
Mapping quantitative studies onto this framework revealed broad conceptual overlap but substantial methodological fragmentation, including heterogeneous and often unvalidated measures.

The extended framework developed through this review provides a more precise foundation for future empirical work examining links between social media use and mental health and highlights the need for research designs capable of capturing the dynamic nature of adolescent social media use.
Almost all teenagers now use social media (e.g., Ofcom, 2024; Park et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Almost all teenagers now use social media (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Ofcom, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Park et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: This near-universal adoption has been met with considerable concern about the potential impact on young people's mental health and wellbeing among news media (Davies et al., 2025; Stern & Burke Odland, 2017), parents and carers (EdChoice, 2023; Ofcom, 2024), policymakers (Department for Digital, 2023; US Surgeon General, 2023), and young people themselves (O'Reilly et al., 2018; Popat & Tarrant, 2022).

text.text: Unsurprisingly, the rapid uptake and associated concerns have also been met with considerable research interest: an umbrella review identified 25 unique reviews examining adolescent social media use and mental health published between 2019 and mid-2021 alone (Valkenburg, Meier, et al., 2022).

text.text: Despite significant interest in the topic, there remains no firm consensus on the impact of social media use on adolescent mental health and wellbeing.
Some researchers suggest social media is one of, if not the most, critical factors in the apparent decline of adolescent mental health, particularly among girls (e.g., Twenge et al., 2022).

text.text: Others, however, argue this rhetoric is extreme and consistent with moral panics observed during previous technological advances, rather than being born out in rigorous evidence (e.g., Orben, 2020a).

text.text: The debate is complicated by the fundamental challenge of defining and measuring social media use.

Indeed, social media are diverse and constantly evolving with myriad possibilities in terms of platforms, content, features, and functions, all of which may reasonably result in varied social media experiences and outcomes.

While academic recognition of this complexity is growing (e.g., Maheux et al., 2025), social media are still commonly conceptualised as a singular construct and the phrase social media is routinely used as a catch-all for all possible uses and platforms (see Buckingham, 2019 for discussion of this issue in the wider context of media studies).

text.text: Perhaps as a result, the field continues to be dominated by coarse measures like overall self-report time spent on social media (Bekalu et al., 2023), which are unreliable (Parry et al., 2021) and tell us very little about the 'active ingredients' that may impact mental health and wellbeing.

text.text: In this scoping review, we aim to move the field forward by systematically identifying and mapping some of those potential ingredients.

In doing so, we seek to provide researchers, practitioners, and other stakeholders with a more nuanced framework for investigating how different forms of social media use may relate to adolescent mental health and wellbeing (Odgers & Jensen, 2020; Valkenburg, Meier, et al., 2022)

text.text: As already described, there is no firm consensus on the impact of social media use on adolescent mental health and wellbeing.

Meta-analyses of (largely) cross-sectional studies tend to find small negative associations, with considerable heterogeneity between studies (e.g., Gabrielle et al., 2024; Ivie et al., 2020; Shannon et al., 2022).

text.text: Some researchers have suggested the relatively small associations and inconsistencies in findings may be due to individual differences in how social media impacts young people.
Indeed, mounting evidence suggests person-specific effects exist (see Maheux et al., 2025 for a review), such that Beyens et al. (2020, p. 1) declared these effects "can no longer be ignored".

text.text: There are several possible types of individual differences that may result in person-specific effects.

For example, differences may plausibly arise from (a) characteristics of young people themselves (e.g., pre-existing mental health and wellbeing, personality traits); (b) the kind of (positive or negative) experiences they have while using social media, and/or (c) how they choose to use social media.
These individual differences are unlikely to operate in isolation.

Rather, they are likely to be mutually reinforcing, with certain patterns of use making particular experiences more or less likely, and individual characteristics shaping both the ways adolescents engage with social media and the kinds of experiences they encounter.
In this review, we focus specifically on what young people do on social media, as this is likely the most amenable component to intervention.

Researchers have started to consider, and examine, the potential importance of differences in what young people do on social media for their mental health and wellbeing (e.g., Thorisdottir et al., 2019; Winstone et al., 2022).

text.text: Nonetheless, understanding of what adolescent social media use actually looks like in practice remains somewhat limited.
Indeed, young people consistently tell us that adults do not understand their social media use (Biernesser et al., 2020; Hjetland et al., 2021; West et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Indeed, young people consistently tell us that adults do not understand their social media use <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Biernesser et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Hjetland et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b81">West et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: This might be, at least in part, because we rarely ask adolescents directly about what they do on social media.

Instead, models and theoretical frameworks have typically focused on the drivers of 'social media addiction' or 'problematic social media use', which borrow from other frameworks, rather than considering subtle differences in how social media are used (Lee et al., 2017; Ngai et al., 2015; Sun & Zhang, 2021).

text.text: Such broad conceptualisations of social media use have, however, provided little consistent evidence regarding the types of social media use that make young people most or least vulnerable to negative outcomes.

For example, while active use has typically been theorised to benefit wellbeing, and passive use to undermine wellbeing (Verduyn et al., 2017; Verduyn et al., 2020), empirical support for this dichotomy is inconsistent.

text.text: Indeed, two recent systematic reviews and meta-analyses found limited and inconsistent support for the passive-use hypothesis, with some analyses finding effects that contradict the hypothesis entirely (Godard & Holtzman, 2024; Valkenburg, van Driel, et al., 2022).

For example, some of the most fundamental social media activities such as liking and commenting on others' posts are inconsistently categorised as both 'passive' and 'active' across different studies (Valkenburg, van Driel, et al., 2022).

text.text: As a result, more and more researchers are now suggesting a movement away from these overly simplistic measures (Beyens et al., 2021; de Vaate et al., 2024; Meier et al., 2024; Meier & Krause, 2022; Valkenburg, van Driel, et al., 2022).

text.text: The shift towards more nuanced conceptualisations of social media use has been accompanied by the development of several theoretical models and frameworks.

Some, such as the Differential Susceptibility to Media Effects Model (Valkenburg & Peter, 2013), focus on explaining who is more or less susceptible to media effects, highlighting the role of dispositional, developmental, and socialcontext factors.

text.text: Other frameworks focus more directly on the processes through which media use may influence mental health and wellbeing.

text.text: More recently, the Digital Media-use Effects model (Liebherr et al., 2025) integrated psychological mechanisms (e.g., one's mood) with proximal (e.g., time of use) and distal contextual factors (e.g., regulatory context) to explain when digital media use may be functional or dysfunctional for children and adolescents' wellbeing.

text.text: However, these frameworks do not provide a framework for systematically characterising the constituent features of social media use itself.
The Multidimensional Model of Social Media Use (MMSMU; Yang et al., 2021) addresses this gap.

text.text: The MMSMU identifies three key dimensions of adolescent social media use that, together, characterise use and enable more accurate predictions about the implications and likely outcomes.
These dimensions include, (1) activities (interactive, active, and passive); (2) motives (enhancement and compensation), and (3) communication partners (strong and weak ties).
Drawing on existing evidence, Yang et al. (2021) demonstrate how individual differences across these dimensions may result in different wellbeing outcomes.

text.text: For example, they suggest that using social media for enhancement (e.g., relationship maintenance) may lead to improved wellbeing, while using social media for compensation (e.g., relationship formation) may lead to poorer wellbeing.

Similarly, they suggest that interactive use (e.g., direct messaging) may lead to improved wellbeing through perceived social support, while passive use (e.g., browsing other-generated content) may harm wellbeing through judgemental social comparison.

The development of the MMSMU represents a critical move forward in the field by providing a formal framework through which researchers and practitioners can identify the kinds of social media use that may make young people most or least vulnerable to negative outcomes.
However, it shares a key limitation with the broader field: a lack of consultation with young people themselves.

Indeed, across adolescent health research more broadly, young people are rarely involved in shaping the research questions or constructs used to study them and are more often consulted only at later stages for feedback on decisions already made (Sellars et al., 2021; Warraitch et al., 2025).

text.text: In this case, this requires identifying how young people actually use social media.

Yet, few measures of social media use have been developed with any consultation with young people, and, to the best of our knowledge, no direct work has specifically sought to map young people's perspectives on what social media use looks like for them.
This creates a potential gap between how adolescents themselves understand and describe their social media use and how researchers operationalise it.

Indeed, researchers may group or simplify social media use in ways that do not reflect the distinctions adolescents make, while adolescents may describe forms of social media use that have received little attention by researchers.

Understanding these points of convergence and divergence is essential for assessing whether existing operationalisations adequately capture the breadth of adolescent social media use and, ultimately, whether they provide a sufficiently accurate basis for investigating which usage patterns are associated with the most positive or negative outcomes.
The current mixed-methods scoping review therefore seeks to map what is already known about how young people use social media.

We operationalise adolescent social media use according to the three dimensions specified by the MMSMU -the activity performed, the motive underlying the activity, and the communication partner involved -and use this as a common conceptual framework through which to map both adolescent-described and researcher-operationalised social media use.
Specifically, we ask three review questions: (1) how do adolescents describe their own social media use?
; (2) how has adolescent social media use been quantified and/or categorised in quantitative research literature?
and (3) to what extent do quantifications and categorisations of adolescent social media use align with how adolescents themselves describe their social media use?

text.text: The search strings (see supplementary file 2) were developed based on the authors' expertise and refined following pilot searches.
To ensure relevance and avoid the risk of false positives, we narrowed the search to titles only.

This was especially pertinent given terms such as "social network" can relate to other unrelated bodies of literature, and that social media are often peripherally referred to in adolescent literature.
The searches were limited to literature published in the English language, and there was no year restriction.
Eligible studies had to present peer-reviewed research (including in empirical book chapters) about how adolescents use social media, beyond the coarse measures outlined in the Introduction.
Both quantitative and qualitative studies were included.
We included doctoral dissertations and theses but excluded dissertations and theses at other levels to maintain quality standards consistent with peerreviewed research.
We excluded conference abstracts due to insufficient detail.
Informants had to be adolescents, with mean participant age between 10 and 24 years, or relevant data from participants in this age range being extractable.

We also excluded studies that used social media as an intervention (e.g., to address mental health), a method to understand other phenomena (e.g., examining what adolescents say on social media about a specific topic), or observational techniques (e.g., analysis of adolescents' social media profiles).
We then applied additional inclusion/exclusion criteria depending on whether articles were qualitative or quantitative in nature.
Qualitative studies had to report first-hand descriptions of adolescent social media use.

The following were excluded: hypothetical or prospective uses; activities adolescents reported not doing or would not do; general affordances without indication of actual use; privacy-related settings or configurations unless directly linked to specific uses (e.g., "posting about feelings on a private account" would be coded, but "setting account to private" would not); and preparatory activities that occur outside social media (e.g., creating videos to later post on social media).
Quantitative studies had to collect self-report data regarding how adolescents use social media, and this data had to be able to be isolated and extracted.

For example, studies only reporting total Bergen Facebook Addiction Scale scores (Andreassen et al., 2012) would be categorised as having relevant but unextractable findings, and therefore excluded, while those isolating and reporting scores on the mood modification sub-scale would be included.

Data charting was done independently, by JD.

As a team, we developed an a priori charting template which included article details (e.g., journal, year), study details (e.g., country/countries of study, aims, design), and participant characteristics (e.g., age, gender, ethnicity).

This was updated following study selection to include the charting of sampling procedure, whether the sample was from the general population or a sub-group (e.g., girls), and details about the social media characteristics (e.g., whether the authors focused on a particular platform).
See supplementary file 2 for the final extraction template.
We did not conduct a formal assessment of the methodological quality, consistent with scoping review methodology (Peters, Godfrey, et al., 2020).

text.text: We charted additional data pertaining to each study's qualitative and/or quantitative components.
For qualitative studies, this included the data generation (e.g., interviews) and data analysis technique(s) used (e.g., thematic analysis).
For quantitative studies, this included the measure(s) of social media use used, the specific social media uses reported, and the type of data reported (e.g., mean score).

We also charted evidence relating to the validity and reliability of measure(s) of social media use used, including the type of validity (e.g., structural validity via exploratory factor analysis) or reliability assessment (e.g., internal consistency via Cronbach's alpha) conducted and, where reported, relevant estimates.

We then classified studies according to how their measure(s) of social media use were developed: 'existing'foot_0 (a previously developed item, scale, or sub-scale with a reference to the original article), 'newly developed' (novel items, scales, or subscales with evidence of scale development practices and validation, e.g., component factor analysis), or 'on-the-fly' (novel items, scales, or sub-scales with no evidence of systematic development or validation, as per Flake & Fried, 2020).

Where quantitative articles categorised groups of users based on their social media use, we also charted details regarding these groups (e.g., the group names as described by the study authors and the uses that characterised each group).

To start, JD read the results sections of all included articles at least twice to obtain a sense of the data (Hsieh & Shannon, 2005).

text.text: During this initial read, she assigned in vivo (i.e., verbatim) codes to words and phrases that illustrated how young people described their social media use (Saldaña, 2021).

text.text: Coding was conducted at a purely semantic level, with no additional interpretation, and was conducted on both direct quotes from young people, and author's descriptions of young people's experiences.

For example, the direct quotation "I had a group project last term, and we did talk about it [on social media]" (West et al., 2023, p. 7) was coded as "talking about group project" while the author report "one participant … regularly update[d her] settings and preferences to avoid exposure to negative or anxiety-provoking content" was coded as "changing settings/preferences to avoid negative or anxiety-provoking content" (Winstone et al., 2023, p. 304).

text.text: In total, this process produced 4,124 in vivo codes.

Following the initial coding, JD exported the in vivo codes into Microsoft Excel for analysis, with a row for each in vivo code and three columns corresponding to the top-level dimensions identified by Yang et al. (2021): (a) the activity, (b) motive, and (c) communication partner(s).

(2021)</ref>: (a) the activity, (b) motive, and (c) communication partner(s).

text.text: Next, she deductively extracted the relevant part of each in vivo code into the appropriate column(s).

Where an in vivo code captured more than one dimension, she extracted the relevant portion into each: for example, "talking to friends" was split into "talking" (activity) and "friends" (communication partner).
Having assigned each in vivo code to the appropriate top-level dimension(s), JD then grouped semantically similar codes within each dimension to generate categories.

Note, while Yang et al. (2021) offer categories within the dimensions (e.g., interactive/active/passive within activity), we decided as a team to adopt an inductive, bottom-up -rather than a deductive, top-down -approach at this stage to avoid missing aspects present in young people's accounts but not present in the model.

(2021)</ref> offer categories within the dimensions (e.g., interactive/active/passive within activity), we decided as a team to adopt an inductive, bottom-up -rather than a deductive, top-down -approach at this stage to avoid missing aspects present in young people's accounts but not present in the model.

text.text: For example, grouping "watching videos", "reading blog posts", and "liking pictures" together, under a broader activity category of "consuming and engaging with content" rather than imposing pre-defined categories of 'active' or 'passive' use.

We also decided, as a team, to avoid making assumptions about underlying motivations for activities, and instead only coded motives when they were explicitly stated, to ensure our findings reflected what young people actually reported rather than our own assumptions or interpretations.
During the coding, JD noticed that some young people described the functions that activities served rather than articulating explicit motives or core activities.

For example, stating they 'express themselves' on social media but not explicitly identifying this as a motive for using social media, or specifying the exact activity through which they do this (e.g., by posting content, by expressing themselves in messages to their friends).

In response, and following discussion with co-authors, we decided to broaden the 'motive' dimension to 'motivational functions', capturing these functional relationships without assuming participants consciously framed them as reasons for action.
Once a full draft of the initial framework had been developed, JD shared this with co-authors for feedback and discussion.
This was an iterative process.

Across seven iterations, we progressively refined the framework as a team, ultimately arriving at five core activities, five overarching motivational functions, and five types of communication partner that sufficiently captured the range described by adolescents across included studies.

Complementing the three dimensions outlined in the MMSMU -and based on Meier et al. (2024) argument regarding the importance of the context surrounding activities -we decided as a team to add an additional coding column to capture, where available, type of content/message being described (e.g., hate speech, humour).

(2024)</ref> argument regarding the importance of the context surrounding activities -we decided as a team to add an additional coding column to capture, where available, type of content/message being described (e.g., hate speech, humour).

text.text: During coding, it became apparent to JD that young people also included other contextual details in their qualitative accounts that were not already captured through the MMSMU dimensions or this additional content column.
For example, when, or under which circumstances the use occurred (e.g., during the summer holidays), and on which kind of account (e.g., main, spam, Finsta).
After discussion as a team, we decided to add additional coding columns to capture these emergent aspects.
JD extracted contextual details (what, when, and where) descriptively, as reported by participants.
Systematic categorisation of contextual factors was beyond the scope of this review (see Limitations), but JD did assess the frequency with which these appeared.
Using the framework generated for RQ1, JD assessed to what extent the measures identified in response to RQ2 reflected adolescents' lived experiences (i.e., addressing RQ3).
This involved deductively coding the items and sub-scales reported in the findings section of each relevant paper against the framework.

For example, an "escapism motive" subscale would be coded as the motive "coping" while an item regarding the use of social media to "chat with friends" would be coded under the core activity "interacting with others", and the communication partner "close personal ties".

JD also kept notes where items and sub-scales could not be coded against the framework, either because they were too broad to map onto the framework, or because they were not present in young people's accounts.

Finally, she compared the frequency of codes across quantitative measures and adolescent descriptions and assessed whether existing measures captured the contextual nuances that featured in adolescents' own accounts of their social media use.

text.text: Six excerpts (0.4%) had to be double coded, resulting in 1,662 data excerpt rows.

Five were double coded because they contained uses that spanned multiple activity categories (e.g., liked/shared posts related to tanning), and one was double coded because it contained multiple motivational functions (escapism + peeking (vicarious lives) motivation).

At this broad category level, all the key elements of the coding framework were present: we identified items and sub-scales that covered each of the five activities, the five motivational functions, and the five communication partners.
However, 77 data excerpts (4.6%) across 47 studies (14.8%) were considered too broad to fit the framework.

Most commonly, these involved excerpts that simply reported on 'active' or 'passive' use, which have the potential to span the range of activities identified in response to RQ1 (e.g., active use could relate to social interaction and/or creating content).
Four excerpts (0.2%) contained elements that did not fit the framework because they were not present in qualitative accounts.
Two assessed whether participants entered social media competitions, and two assessed a sexual motive for sexting.
As such, in total, 1,585 of the 1,662 data excerpts (95.4%) mapped onto the framework.

We also examined whether mapped excerpts included any of the additional contextual elements identified within young people's qualitative accounts (e.g., what was involved, when it occurred, on which account it took place).

text.text: of adolescent social media use align with adolescents' lived experiences?
At the broadest (category) level, we identified promising overlap between what adolescents described doing on social media in qualitative studies, and what was measured in quantitative research.

Indeed, all the activity types, motivational functions, and communication partners identified in adolescents' first-hand accounts were also present in quantitative measures, suggesting young people and researchers share an understanding regarding the most critical forms of adolescent social media use.
The specific activities, functions and communication partners were also mentioned with similar frequency across both adolescent first-hand accounts, and quantitative studies (see Table 5).

Nonetheless, there were some differences.
Contextual details regarding where activities occurred (e.g., spam accounts, Finstas) were nearly absent from quantitative studies (0.06% vs.
2.5% in qualitative accounts), despite adolescents describing how they adapted their behaviour across different account types.
Similarly, quantitative measures appeared to devote less attention to communication partners than adolescent first-hand accounts (19.9% vs.
25.7% in qualitative accounts).
Which communication partners were discussed and/or measured also differed.
Adolescents most commonly spoke about close personal ties and identity and affinity ties.
In contrast, quantitative studies gave relatively more weight to weak ties (19.9% vs.
8.3% in qualitative accounts) and aspirational ties (18.0% vs.
8.2% in qualitative accounts), while identity and affinity ties were less well represented (7.9% vs.
13.1% in qualitative accounts).
Following peer review, we conducted post-hoc comparisons stratifying the findings by developmental period to examine whether the patterns described above held consistently across development.

To do so, we examined four periods: middle childhood (which we defined as age 10), early adolescence (age 11-13), middle adolescence (14-17), and emerging adulthood (18-24) (e.g., Arnett, 2000; Salmela-Aro, 2011).

text.text: Note, we acknowledge that these periods are not discretely bounded, and exact age ranges vary across the literature.
We use them here as a heuristic for examining whether patterns differ across broad developmental stages, rather than as precise cut-offs.

The stratified analysis revealed similar patterns of overlap and divergence within each period, indicating that the areas of convergence and divergence noted above hold across development rather than reflecting an artefact of pooling across a wide age range.

Some notable developmental trends were also apparent: creating and managing content increased steadily in prevalence from middle childhood through emerging adulthood in both qualitative and quantitative studies, while interacting with others and reliance on close personal ties showed the opposite pattern, decreasing across the same developmental span.

As outlined in the Introduction, social media use has been traditionally conceptualised and operationalised through relatively coarse lenses, such as time spent or broad categories of active/passive use.
More recently, there has been growing recognition that social media use is a complex and multidimensional phenomenon (e.g., Liebherr et al., 2025; Maheux et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2021).
text.formatted: More recently, there has been growing recognition that social media use is a complex and multidimensional phenomenon (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Liebherr et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Maheux et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b85">Yang et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Our findings add to this growing body of work by illustrating the sheer diversity of adolescent social media use.

Young people described their use as spanning a wide range of activities, motivational functions, and communication partners, involving a range of content types, taking place during a range of different times and in various different (online) places.
Importantly, they also described how these factors interact to create a vast and heterogenous set of possible social media uses.
Indeed, the core activities we identified were rarely confined to a single motive.

For example, young people reported consuming and engaging with content to feel a sense of belonging (social and identity-oriented function), be entertained (fun and relaxation function), distract themselves from negative emotions (coping function), learn something new (learning, growth and future-oriented function), and to reflect on their memories (practical function).

Equally, young people said they engaged in a range of activities to fulfil each and any of these motives: some reported interacting with others to help them cope, while others created content, and/or consumed other people's content for the same purpose.
Understanding this multidimensionality is crucial, as particular combinations of activities, motives, and communication partners may carry distinct implications for mental health.
For example, "consuming and engaging with content" tells us little without knowing whose content one is consuming, or what the content represents.

Preliminary research supports these distinctions: experimental and cross-sectional self-report data suggests that viewing 'fitspiration' content is associated with negative body image and disordered eating behaviours (Holland & Tiggemann, 2017; Prichard et al., 2020), whereas engaging with body positivity content is associated with improved body image and wellbeing (Cohen et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Preliminary research supports these distinctions: experimental and cross-sectional self-report data suggests that viewing 'fitspiration' content is associated with negative body image and disordered eating behaviours <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Holland & Tiggemann, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">Prichard et al., 2020)</ref>, whereas engaging with body positivity content is associated with improved body image and wellbeing <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Cohen et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Equally, "coping" as a motivational function carries different implications depending on how one is using social media to cope.

For example, engaging with communities who share similar challenges may foster a sense of connection and validation (Craig & McInroy, 2014; Naslund et al., 2016; Wargo, 2017) while consuming aspirational content -possibly as a way to escape, or live vicariously through others -is associated with social comparison and poorer body image (Choukas-Bradley et al., 2022; Pedalino & Camerini, 2022).

text.text: Without accounting for these distinctions, research risks conflating potentially beneficial and harmful uses under one umbrella.
Our findings also reveal how social media is now embedded in everyday psychological and social functions that were previously fulfilled through other means.
Young people described using social media to rant, vent, and express emotions, with some explicitly comparing their social media use to keeping a diary/journal.
Notably, some created completely anonymous or private accounts (with no followers) specifically for this purpose, treating social media as a personal outlet rather than a social space.
Similarly, some young people spoke of using social media to store and organise memories, functioning much like traditional photo albums.
These examples illustrate how social media platforms have absorbed (non-social) functions once served by analogue practices.
Conversely, we also observed that seemingly solitary activities on social media often served social purposes.

For example, young people described posting content to share their opinions with others, to publicly illustrate important relationships, or to reassure significant others about their wellbeing and activities.
This inverse pattern -where ostensibly individual actions function as social gestures -further complicates our understanding of what constitutes 'social' media.
Most definitions of social media emphasise connection and communication between users (Aichner et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Most definitions of social media emphasise connection and communication between users <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Aichner et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Yet, our findings illustrate that the 'social' in social media is neither stable nor straightforward, and that, ultimately, these definitions have failed to keep pace with platform evolution (see also Feldkamp, 2021; Novak, 2020 for discussion of TikTok as an 'anti-social' social media platform).
text.formatted: Yet, our findings illustrate that the 'social' in social media is neither stable nor straightforward, and that, ultimately, these definitions have failed to keep pace with platform evolution (see also <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Feldkamp, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Novak, 2020</ref> for discussion of TikTok as an 'anti-social' social media platform).

text.text: In light of this apparent conceptual lag, collaborative work with stakeholders (e.g., young people, educators, policymakers, and practitioners) may be required to develop shared understandings of social media that reflect how platforms are actually used today.
The complexity and diversity of adolescent social media use highlighted above necessitates a more granular framework than currently exists.

By drawing directly on adolescents' own accounts, we were able to expand Yang et al.'s (2021) MMSMU to offer a more precise and context-sensitive framework for understanding In addition to expanding the three dimensions of the MMSMU, we identified three contextual elements largely absent from the original model: what is involved (e.g., content consumed, topic of conversation), when or under which circumstances the use takes place (e.g., during the school holidays, in the presence of a friend), and where (i.e., on which account).

text.text: These elements echo aspects of other theoretical frameworks of digital media use (e.g., Liebherr et al., 2025; Livingstone et al., 2018), though they remain unaccounted for, at least formally, within the MMSMU itself.

text.text: Given that these features were present in more than half of adolescents' accounts (52.0%), we suggest they represent fundamental aspects of adolescent social media use, rather than incidental details that theoretical models can afford to overlook.
Promisingly, quantitative studies also frequently captured these details (47.4% of measurement excerpts), demonstrating wider recognition of their importance.

Taken together, our findings allow us to move beyond treating adolescent social media use as a singular behaviour and towards a more precise conceptual definition, addressing the challenges outlined in the Introduction.

We define adolescent social media use as a multidimensional and context-dependent phenomenon arising from the specific combination of activities, motivational functions, communication partners, and types of content, which are situated within specific accounts or platforms, and embedded in wider situational contexts (e.g., who the adolescent is physically with, where they are, and ongoing local or world events that shape these dimensions).

Crucially, these dimensions do not appear to operate independently or combine additively; rather, their meaning depends on how they are configured in relation to one another and to the surrounding context.

As such, adolescent social media use, and any potential links between this use and mental health and wellbeing, are unlikely to be adequately understood by reducing use to a single summary indicator, as is the norm in the current literature (Sursely et al., 2026).
text.formatted: As such, adolescent social media use, and any potential links between this use and mental health and wellbeing, are unlikely to be adequately understood by reducing use to a single summary indicator, as is the norm in the current literature <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">(Sursely et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: This carries clear implications for how the construct is operationalised and measured in future studies.
We suggest two ways this might be achieved.

First, researchers may use existing theory, empirical evidence, and/or insights from young people themselves to identify the particular activities, motivational functions, communication partners, content types, accounts, and/or contextual features that are likely to be relevant to a given outcome.
Alternatively, where the aim is to understand social media use more holistically, measures and analytic techniques that capture multiple components simultaneously may be more appropriate.

For example, multidimensional measures encompassing several aspects of use, person-centred approaches like latent profile analysis, or network analysis approaches that explicitly model the interplay between dimensions.
The dimensions of social media use identified here should also be considered in relation to development.

Adolescence is characterised by a number of developmental processes that may shape how young people use social media, including identity formation, increasing autonomy from parents, and heightened salience of peer relationships (Steinberg & Morris, 2001; Steinberg, 2014).
text.formatted: Adolescence is characterised by a number of developmental processes that may shape how young people use social media, including identity formation, increasing autonomy from parents, and heightened salience of peer relationships <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">(Steinberg & Morris, 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">Steinberg, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Many of the activities, motivational functions, and communication partners identified in the present review map closely onto these developmental processes.

For example, adolescents frequently described using social media to explore and express aspects of their identity, maintain peer relationships, and seek belonging among identity-and affinity-based communities.

These findings suggest that the forms of use identified here may reflect the particular developmental challenges and opportunities that characterise adolescence, rather than universal patterns of engagement that would be expected to hold across all groups.
As such, the framework proposed here should be understood as a model of adolescent social media use, rather than a general model applicable across the lifespan.

Future research may seek to examine which dimensions of the framework, if any, are developmentally specific and which generalise across age groups, as well as whether the relationships between dimensions change across development.
At the highest level, we identified overlap between the social media uses that adolescents described in qualitative studies, and those measured in quantitative research.

This alignment is encouraging because it suggests that quantitative measures have, at minimum, face validity: they capture the activities, motivational functions, and communication partners that adolescents themselves identify as central to their social media experience.
This is a promising, since face validity is a foundational requirement for measurement validity (Flake & Fried, 2020).
text.formatted: This is a promising, since face validity is a foundational requirement for measurement validity <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Flake & Fried, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: There are several potential explanations for such convergence.
First, some of the existing measures utilised could have been generated with input from young people, meaning the content was already grounded in their first-hand experiences.

Second, as outlined in section 4.4, adolescent social media use may, at least in part, reflect key developmental processes which are already well understood and therefore readily recognised by researchers working within both traditions.
Third, some of the uses identified here may reflect common platform affordances that are built into basic platform design and are therefore obvious enough to be captured consistently.
In any case, we assert this broad convergence should be interpreted cautiously.

Indeed, alignment can only be certified at the highest categorical level, and it was beyond the scope of this review to assess whether which individual activities (e.g., posting, within creating and managing content), motivational functions (e.g., attention seeking, within social and identity-oriented), or communication partners (e.g., classmates, within extended ties) appeared with comparable frequency across qualitative and quantitative studies.

Moreover, although we examined how frequently each contextual dimension was represented across the two research traditions, it was out of scope to examine the specific features captured within these dimensions (e.g., whether qualitative and quantitative studies captured similar types of content).
Such an examination may reveal important gaps regarding what has been prioritised for measurement, beyond the broad categories where alignment is evident.
Importantly, the comparison also revealed areas where qualitative and quantitative approaches diverged.
First, only one item in one quantitative study assessed which account an activity took place on: a cancer-specific account.

Yet, in their qualitative first-hand accounts, young people described maintaining multiple accounts (e.g., 'main' and 'spam' accounts) for different purposes, with sensitive (e.g., emotional or identity expression) and risky (e.g., content regarding illegal or antisocial activities) content more likely to occur on secondary accounts, and more 'polished' content on widely accessible accounts.

Emerging work on 'Finstas' suggests these secondary accounts may be common, particularly among adolescent girls who use them to manage context collapse by presenting more authentic selves to smaller groups of close friends (e.g., Kang & Wei, 2020; Tao & Ellison, 2023).
text.formatted: Emerging work on 'Finstas' suggests these secondary accounts may be common, particularly among adolescent girls who use them to manage context collapse by presenting more authentic selves to smaller groups of close friends (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Kang & Wei, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">Tao & Ellison, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: However, systematic research on prevalence, motivations, and outcomes remains sparse.
This may be an important avenue for future research.
Stakeholders should also recognise that alternative accounts often host more sensitive or risky material, and thus surface-level observations of adolescents' primary accounts may be incomplete.
The use of multiple accounts also has implications for research.
At present, it is not clear which account(s) adolescents have in mind when they respond to general survey items.

For example, a young person who never posts on their 'main' account but uploads daily to a private 'spam' account could respond to an item about posting in several ways: they might indicate that they never post if they are thinking of their main account, that they post frequently if they are thinking of their spam account, or that they sometimes post if trying to average across both.
This ambiguity complicates the interpretation of self-report data on social media use.
If researchers cannot be sure which account participants are thinking of, it becomes difficult to accurately assess activities such as posting frequency, engagement, or exposure to content.
Consequently, findings about adolescents' social media use may reflect measurement artefacts, rather than true differences in use.
The second area of distinction centred around the types of communication partner that were prioritised.
More than 13% of the qualitative codes that included a communication partner referenced identity and affinity ties (i.e., "other people like me"), compared to just 8% of the quantitative codes.
Conversely, just 8% of qualitative codes that included a communication partner referenced aspirational ties (e.g., celebrities, influencers) compared to 18% of quantitative codes.

The quantitative emphasis on aspirational ties may reflect researchers' focus on potential negative impacts (e.g., the effects of influencers on body image and social comparison; Choukas-Bradley et al., 2022; Pedalino & Camerini, 2022) which have also garnered attention in public health policy (e.g., House of Commons Women and Equalities Committee, 2021; US Surgeon General, 2023).

text.text: Our findings suggest this focus on aspirational ties, however, may have come at the expense of examining identity and affinity ties which could play a more central role in users' day-to-day experiences and may offer protective or beneficial effects (e.g., through community building, peer support, and validation of shared experiences).
Alternatively, this discrepancy could reflect differences in sampling approaches.
Indeed, 40% of qualitative studies employed sub-group sampleswhere identity and affinity ties may be particularly salient and important (e.g.,
LGBTQ+ young people, Craig & McInroy, 2014; Wargo, 2017) -compared to just 15% of quantitative studies.

text.text: Nonetheless, this sampling difference itself raises important questions about whose social media experiences inform our understanding, and whether broad quantitative measures adequately capture the experiences of populations for whom identity-based online communities serve crucial functions for wellbeing and social support.
Addressing these questions will require both more inclusive sampling in quantitative research and measures sensitive to the diverse ways different groups engage with social media.
We also identified several methodological concerns that may compromise our ability to understand how adolescent social media use relates to mental health and wellbeing.
More than half of the quantitative studies (54%) used measures that were developed 'on-the-fly' (i.e., with no evidence of systematic development or validation) (Flake & Fried, 2020).
text.formatted: More than half of the quantitative studies (54%) used measures that were developed 'on-the-fly' (i.e., with no evidence of systematic development or validation) <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Flake & Fried, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: This is perhaps unsurprising given the rapid pace and scale of change in adolescent social media use.

Rigorous measure development is a lengthy process, and researchers working in such a fast-moving field face a trade-off between waiting for a validated instrument and studying a version of social media that may no longer reflect adolescents' current experience by the time it is ready.
Nonetheless, this trade-off does not remove the need to assess quality, and without evidence of systematic development or validation, the quality of these measures simply remains unknown.

We assert that the field would benefit from clearer guidance on what constitutes acceptable minimum standards for measure development and reporting when full-scale validation is not feasible, analogous to approaches adopted in other fields facing similar time pressures (e.g., rapid guideline development in evidence-based medicine; Kowalski et al., 2018).
text.formatted: We assert that the field would benefit from clearer guidance on what constitutes acceptable minimum standards for measure development and reporting when full-scale validation is not feasible, analogous to approaches adopted in other fields facing similar time pressures (e.g., rapid guideline development in evidence-based medicine; <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Kowalski et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Where existing measures were used, there was no clear consensus regarding which to use: we identified the use of more than 80 different instruments across the 111 studies using existing measures.
An additional 48 studies developed entirely new measures of social media use.
In total, this means that across 321 quantitative studies, we identified almost 130 different measures of adolescent social media use, roughly one distinct measure for every three studies conducted.

This extraordinary proliferation of measures makes it difficult, if not impossible, to compare findings across studies or conduct systematic reviews to determine, for example, which specific uses are most commonly associated with indicators of mental health and wellbeing.
This fragmentation is compounded by concerns regarding the overall quality of measures being used.
Only one-quarter (25%) of the quantitative studies assessed the validity of the measure(s) of social media use they used.
This reduces to just 12% when excluding measure-development studies, which, by our definition, had to provide evidence of validation.
Less than half of the studies (48%) assessed reliability.
Where reliability was assessed, internal consistency varied widely (α = .33 to .97), with some studies utilising measures with demonstrably poor reliability (Tavakol & Dennick, 2011).
text.formatted: Where reliability was assessed, internal consistency varied widely (α = .33 to .97), with some studies utilising measures with demonstrably poor reliability <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">(Tavakol & Dennick, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: This is a critical concern.

If our measures do not validly capture what adolescents actually do on social media, or if they produce inconsistent results, then the associations we observe between social media use and mental health and wellbeing may be artefactual or worse, misleading, ultimately limiting our ability to draw meaningful conclusions.
Worse still, potential interventions developed on the basis of these findings risk being misdirected and could inadvertently undermine rather than support adolescents.
The overall design of quantitative studies presents additional challenges.
The vast majority of included quantitative studies (86%) used cross-sectional designs which do not allow researchers to draw causal inferences (see also, Orben, 2020b).
Among the few longitudinal studies, half (53%) used only two waves of data collection, with relatively brief follow-up periods.

Yet, two-wave designs provide minimal advantages over cross-sectional work: they can establish temporal precedence but create "half-longitudinal" designs where portions of causal pathways remain cross-sectional, failing to account for autoregressive effects and mediating processes (Cole & Maxwell, 2003; Maxwell et al., 2011).
text.formatted: Yet, two-wave designs provide minimal advantages over cross-sectional work: they can establish temporal precedence but create "half-longitudinal" designs where portions of causal pathways remain cross-sectional, failing to account for autoregressive effects and mediating processes <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Cole & Maxwell, 2003;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Maxwell et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: As such, longer-term longitudinal research is undoubtedly needed to better understand developmental trajectories and potential bidirectional relationships between social media use and mental health and wellbeing.
Nonetheless, qualitative data from this review suggests even well-designed longitudinal studies may miss critical dynamics if they rely on infrequent assessments and retrospective self-reports.

As outlined in 4.3, adolescents described social media use as fluid and context-dependent, shifting across activities, platforms, accounts, and communication partners throughout the day and even within individual sessions, in response to changing moods and social contexts.

This dynamic quality suggests that adolescent social media use may be better conceptualised as a fluctuating, moment-to-moment process rather than a stable behaviour that can be meaningfully aggregated over long periods.

Moreover, evidence from screen time research demonstrates that retrospective self-reports are often inaccurate, with substantial discrepancies between self-reported and device-logged usage (Parry et al., 2021; Verbeij et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Moreover, evidence from screen time research demonstrates that retrospective self-reports are often inaccurate, with substantial discrepancies between self-reported and device-logged usage <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Parry et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b76">Verbeij et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: As such, asking young people to retrospectively recall and summarise their social media use over days, weeks, or months may obscure important variability and fail to capture the proximal, context-specific associations between particular types of social media use and momentary wellbeing states.
Intensive longitudinal methods such as ecological momentary assessment (Shiffman et al., 2008) may be better suited to capturing such proximal, context-specific associations.
text.formatted: Intensive longitudinal methods such as ecological momentary assessment <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">(Shiffman et al., 2008)</ref> may be better suited to capturing such proximal, context-specific associations.

text.text: Data donation studies -where participants willingly share their social media data, including time spent on specific platforms, as well as posts liked, shared, or commented on -may also be a fruitful method for acquiring rich, ecologically valid data regarding what young people are engaging with on social media (see Yap et al., 2025 for discussion of feasibility in this context).

text.text: This scoping review provides a comprehensive map of adolescent social media use.
Nonetheless, several limitations should be noted.
First, to maintain a manageable scope within a vast body of literature, we restricted the search to article titles only.
This restriction ensured high relevance but may have inadvertently excluded some relevant studies where social media use was not the primary focus.

Second, although screening was conducted in duplicate, data extraction and inductive coding were performed by a single reviewer (JD), with key analytic decisions discussed and agreed with the wider author team throughout (see Methods).
Due to resource constraints, it was not possible to conduct independent reliability checks of data extraction or coding.
Nonetheless, we sought to mitigate this through our coding approach, remaining at a semantic level without adding interpretation, and through regular discussion with co-authors.
Three additional limitations should be considered in relation to the proposed updates to the MMSMU (Yang et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Three additional limitations should be considered in relation to the proposed updates to the MMSMU <ref type="bibr" target="#b85">(Yang et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: First, the framework outlined is necessarily constrained by what researchers chose to ask young people and subsequently report in their studies.
Important aspects of adolescent social media use may therefore be missing.
Second, all qualitative analysis requires interpretation, and the process of coding and subsequently grouping codes necessarily involves subjectivity (Saldaña, 2021).

We identified a range of qualitative studies (k=229) that captured adolescents' first-hand accounts of their social media use, as well as quantitative studies (k=321) that measured and categorised this use.

With representation from 96 countries across the Global North and South, and participants spanning the full range of adolescence, this review provides a comprehensive picture of adolescent social media use as understood by research to date.

In gathering and synthesising this evidence, we extendYang et al.'s (2021) Multidimensional Model of Social Media Use, offering greater precision to its three dimensions (activity, motive, communication partner), based on young people's own accounts.

text.text: In the sections that follow, we reflect on what our findings reveal about the strengths and limitations of existing research and outline key directions for future inquiry.

Whereas the original model distinguished between three activity types (interactive, active, passive), two types of motive (enhancement and compensation), and two types of communication partner (strong and weak ties), our expanded framework includes five core activities, five types of motivational function, and five groups of communication partner, providing greater precision across each dimension.
Importantly, these expanded ideas are grounded in young people's own accounts, offering a framework that more closely reflects their lived experiences.

Third, while we identified three additional contextual dimensions (what, when, and where), it was beyond the scope of this review to develop systematic categorisations within them.
In light of these limitations, we suggest future research directly engages with adolescents to validate and refine the model proposed here.

Such participatory research should examine (a) whether adolescents recognise these groupings as meaningful distinctions in their own experience; (b) whether important activities, motivational functions, or communication partners have been overlooked; and (c)how adolescents themselves would organise and label the additional contextual elements identified.

One feasible approach would be a member-checking or codesign study, in which adolescents review the proposed framework (e.g., via workshops or focus groups) and provide feedback on its accuracy, completeness, and relevance to their own experience, with the framework iteratively revised based on this input.

Such work could also incorporate reflective elements, inviting adolescents to consider how the activities, motivations, and contexts identified here relate to their own self-perceived wellbeing or behaviour change over time (e.g., through diary or EMA methods that capture in-the-moment reflections on specific instances of social media use, rather than retrospective self-report alone).

Only through such collaboration can we ensure conceptual models truly reflect adolescents' lived experiences.4.8 ConclusionThis scoping review synthesised over 500 studies to map current research on adolescent social media use.
Adolescents described their social media use as complex, fluid, and multi-dimensional, involving diverse activities, motivational functions, and communication partners.

Quantitative research showed promising conceptual overlap with these accounts but often suffered from methodological limitations, including the use of unvalidated measures, and cross-sectional designs that preclude causal inference.

The extraordinary proliferation of different measures prevents meaningful comparison across studies, ultimately compromising efforts to determine which specific uses relate to mental health and wellbeing.
Progress in the field now depends on building consensus around valid, theoretically grounded measures of adolescent social media use.
It also requires more innovative research designs that can capture the fluid, context-dependent nature of adolescent social media use.
Only by addressing these limitations can we reliably identify when, why and for whom social media impacts adolescent mental health and wellbeing.
